newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Over 100 Sri Lankan rebels said killed in battle.
newsitem.headline: Over 100 Sri Lankan rebels said killed in battle.

text.p: Sri Lankan security forces have captured a northern town held by Tamil Tiger rebels after fierce air and artillery attacks, military officials said on Sunday.
The town of Nedunkeni, on the eastern flank of an army push into guerrilla territory in the northern Wanni region, had been the scene of fierce fighting for three days.
"We have captured Nedunkeni," military spokesman Brigadier Tissa Jayatunga told Reuters. "More than 100 terrorists are believed killed, including three intelligence leaders."
Security forces destroyed four camps of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), he said, adding that details of army casualties in the Nedunkeni battle would be released later.

Two army divisions were on the move on separate axes trying to open a land supply route linking Vavuniya, 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo, with Jaffna peninsula, about 100 km (60 miles) further north, military officials said.
The LTTE have accused the military of killing Tamil civilians and destroying property in the guise of opening up a supply route.
The military now depends on costly and tenuous air and sea links to supply their bases and civilians in Jaffna.

The Defence Ministry has only said the main aim of the drive was to capture areas in the shrub-covered Wanni from the LTTE, who are waging a war for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east.
Troops, backed by tanks, artillery and air cover, on Saturday secured the town of Omanthai, 14 km (nine miles) north of Vavuniya, after beating off a rebel counter-attack.
They are now pushing further north, heading towards the heavily fortified rebel-held town of Puliyankulam.
Civilians who fled Nedunkeni, about 40 km (25 miles) northeast of Vavuniya, said the army shelled rebel positions in the area for almost a week.
"There was heavy shell fire and fighting on Thursday," said Sangarapillai Selvaratnam, 43, a farmer after arriving in Vavuniya. "Suddenly, the army marched into the town with tanks."
He was among 35 people, including women and children, brought by the army to Vavuniya on Friday.
Vavuniya government agent K. Ganesh said accommodation and meals were being provided and many more refugees were expected.
International aid agencies which met in Colombo on Saturday asked the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to rush food and shelter to displaced civilians in the Wanni.
The LTTE's clandestine Voice of Tigers radio station, monitored by Reuters, said Nedunkeni was pounded by artillery and air force planes and many civilians had been displaced.
"Many civilians are living under trees," the radio said.

The London-based Tamil Centre for Human Rights said in a statement they had appealed to British Prime Minister Tony Blair to condemn the offensive which they said was a "plan of genocide of Tamils...pursued by successive Sinhalese governments since Sri Lanka's independence from Britain."
Military officials said that by Saturday 40 soldiers and more than 128 rebels had been killed in the offensive, code-named "Jaya Sikuru," or "Sure of Victory", launched on Tuesday.
The LTTE say the army routinely exaggerates rebel casualties.
Hospital officials said some 320 soldiers had been wounded.
Journalists have not yet been allowed in the battle zone.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war, now in its 14th year. The LTTE say the toll is higher.
